As cassis said, the OSI model is very helpful for this.

Basically, let's say an application has the data it is interested in, and let's call that D.

And that application uses some protocol like TCP or UDP (or something else) to communicate to the other computer. Which means we wrap D with TCP in this example. TCP(D)

It knows it wants to send this data to some other machine, using an IP address. So the application calls the OS to send D to the IP. Which is done by wrapping the previously wrapped TCP(D) with IP. IP(TCP(D))

Now the OS takes this and gives it to its network adapter, which wraps that packet for the specific medium it is sending over, most commonly ethernet, but of course there are other protocols. So we continue to wrap the data further: E(IP(TCP(D)))

And finally, we get the physical layer, where we send the individual bits over a wire or through the air. Which we can consider to also be wrapped as there are physical data transmission protocols as well. So all the data our packet has now is P(E(IP(TCP(D))))

The physical layer wrapping is removed once it gets the router, so the packet is now E(IP(TCP(D))).

Then the ethernet layer is removed as the router's firmware needs the IP to know where to send it. IP(TCP(D))

It figures it out and then rewraps them to send to the target computer. E(IP(TCP(D))) P(E(IP(TCP(D))))

It is then received by the target computer (we are assuming on same local network). E(IP(TCP(D)))

That computer's network adapter strips it's layer and passes it to the OS. IP(TCP(D))

The OS then determines if this packet was sent correctly/has no errors. Then passes it to the program that owns that IP:port combination. As well as handle the protocol details, which is more important for TCP than UDP. D

And now the program on the remote machine has received the packet from the origin machine.

So to return to your question. Each layer only cares about its layer. It is given some data to send and a target, which it uses to construct its packet header, which is strip on the receiving end's layer. And as seen by the example, some layers are constantly being stripped and rewrapped. So all of the frame is desired, a lot of thought goes into what is needed by a protocol a layer.

As for the strength of the signal, that highly depends on the physical medium that is used to transmit the data. So networking over a low bandwidth radio signal is going to be much harder than using ethernet.

I think my question got lost in the details. What I want to know is what percentage of the total frame is used on these layers of addressing. Recent googling suggests that it's about 2%, but I was surprised to find I didn't know how big a frame was, etc.

That also greatly depends on the application sending the data. Sending a single byte of data means most of the frame is headers. Sending the maximum size (which can depend on the network) means that the headers probably have the figure you found.

So you are likely interested how the big the headers are in the MTU. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_transmission_unit
